Ishfaq Ahmad Wani ... Petitioner(S)
 Through: - Mr. M. Y. Parray, Advocate.
Vs.
Ut Of J&K & Anr. ...Respondent(S)
 Through: - Mr. Syed Musaib, Dy.AG-for R1.
 Respondent No.2 present in person.
Coram: Hon'Ble Mr. Justice Sanjay Dhar, Judge
 Order
In the present petition, the subject matter of challenge is FIR No.35 of 2024 for offences under Section 323, 354 and 498A of IPC registered with P/S Beerwa and the proceedings emanating therefrom.

2) As per contents of the impugned FIR, complainant Ruqiya (respondent No.2 herein), who happens to be wife of the petitioner, lodged a written report with Police Station Beerwa, against accused (petitioner herein) and his father Ghulam Rasool Wani, alleging therein that on 10.04.2024,
after offering Eid prayers, she was at her home and when the accused (petitioner herein) returned home, he caught hold of her, gave a beating to her, tore apart her clothes and dragged her out of the house.
When she approached accused Ghulam Rasool Wani for help, her husband again caught hold of her and cut her hair with scissor and threw her out of the house.
On the basis of this report, the impugned FIR was registered and investigation was set into motion.
After investigation Page |2 of the case, offences under Sections 323, 354 and 498-A of IPC were found established against the accused.
The challan in the case is stated to be pending before the Court of Additional Special Mobile Magistrate, Beerwa.

sentences.text: It seems that during pendency of the aforesaid proceedings, the parties have entered into a compromise.
They have produced a copy of the compromise deed before this Court.
4) Issue notice to the respondents.
Mr. Syed Musaib, Dy AG, enters appearances and accepts notice on behalf of respondent No.1.
Respondent No.2, who is present in person, accepts notice.

5) In support of the deed of compromise, the statements of the petitioner and the complainant Ruqiya Akhter (respondent No.2 herein) have been recorded by the Registrar Judicial wherein they have stated that they have amicably settled their dispute and that they have no grievance against each other.

6) The petitioners have contended that so far as the case arising out of impugned FIR is concerned,
the same could not be compounded because some of the offences disclosed therein are non-compoundable in nature.
It is in these circumstances that the petitioners have approached this Court for seeking quashment of the aforesaid FIR and the proceedings emanating therefrom.
Page |3 8)
So far as the facts alleged in the petition, particularly those pertaining to the compromise arrived at between the parties, are concerned, the same are not in dispute.

In the backdrop of aforesaid facts, the question arises as to whether this Court has power to quash the proceedings, particularly when some of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused are non-compoundable in nature.

9) It is a settled law that the offences arising out of the disputes where the wrong is basically private or personal in nature like disputes arising out of matrimony and the parties have resolved their entire dispute, the High Court will be within its jurisdiction to quash the criminal proceedings,
particularly when, as a consequence of the compromise arrived at between the parties, there is remote possibility of securing conviction of the accused.

In my aforesaid view, I am fortified by the judgments of the Supreme Court in the cases of Gian Singh. v. State of Punjab & another, (2012) 10 SCC 303 and Narinder Singh & Ors. Vs. State of Punjab & anr, (2014) 6 SCC 466.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Narinder Singh & Ors. Vs. State of Punjab & anr, (2014) 6 SCC 466
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 10) Adverting to the facts of the instant case, it is clear that the parties have entered into a compromise wherein the complainant has categorically stated that she is not willing to pursue the impugned criminal proceedings and that the parties have settled their disputes amicably.

It is also pertinent to mention here that the petitioner and the complainant are closely related to each other and the offences alleged exclusively arise out of matrimonial dispute between the complainant and her husband.

In these circumstances, if an end is not put to the Page |4 criminal proceedings, it would amount to giving a fresh lease of life to the dispute between close relatives which has been settled by them amicably.
It will amount to frittering away of the fruits of compromise that has been arrived at between the parties.
The continuance of criminal proceedings against the accused/petitioner in these circumstances, will be nothing but an abuse of process of law.
